one_liner: Maintained build of RealNetworks' Helix MP3 encoder, reputed (not measured here) to encode several times faster than LAME.
what_it_does: hmp3 packages the 1995-2005 Helix MP3 (MPEG-1/2 Layer III) encoder so it builds with a current gcc on Linux x86-64 and ARM, plus Visual Studio 2015 projects, and adds a LAME-style Xing/Info tag, Wave64/RF64 input, VBR bitrate limits and resampling fixes. It ships as the hmp3 command-line tool (WAV in, MP3 out, VBR by default, -B is per-channel CBR bitrate) and a static library whose API is the C++ class CMp3Enc: fill an E_CONTROL struct, call L3_audio_encode_init or MP3_audio_encode_init, then feed 1152-sample frames. It is not a drop-in for libmp3lame's lame_* API.
how_it_is_fast: The default acoustic model (CMp3Enc::L3acousticQuick) works on the MDCT energies the encoder already computed ('uses xform energy only, pcm not used'): emapLong/emapShort plus a spreading/SMR pass, with no separate FFT psychoacoustic model, while LAME runs an FFT-based psymodel and iterative noise-shaping loops. Quantization uses table-driven arithmetic: x^(3/4) built from IEEE-754 exponent/mantissa lookup tables in pow34.c (hence -DIEEE_FLOAT), and a fast-rounding inner loop in l3math.c's noise estimate. The Linux build is plain C/C++ at -O3 with LTO (about 3% gain per the commit log); the original i386 assembly in hmp3/src/platform/win/i386 is not used by the Makefile.
when_to_use: Bulk transcoding of large libraries to MP3 where encode time per CPU core matters and you can accept a different quality profile from LAME
VBR at mid-to-high bitrates (default about 128 kbps VBR; -V100 -HF2 gives about 185 kbps) for 32/44.1/48 kHz stereo music
Embedding an MP3 encoder in a C++ program whose distribution can carry RPSL source-release terms for the encoder directory
Server-side encoding where an x86-64-v3 or znver4 build with PGO is acceptable (fork timings show at most about 1.25x over a plain gcc build, 7.43 s to 5.92 s)
when_not_to_use: Low bitrates: CBR below about 48 kbps per channel fails with ENCODER INIT FAIL (issue #8, open since 2025-01), and LAME handles 80 kbps stereo at 32 kHz
Projects that need LAME's API, presets, ReplayGain, ID3 tagging or bit-exact outputs: hmp3 has none of these, and march/fast-math builds change the encoded bytes
When you need a measured speed or quality claim: no benchmark against LAME exists in the repository, its issues or its fork
GPL-only or permissive-only codebases: the encoder is under RPSL-1.0 (reciprocal, not GPL-compatible) or RCSL, and only files outside hmp3/ are MIT
Long-term maintenance needs: last commit 2024-05-31, single maintainer, 38 stars

integration.form: static lib (libhmp3.a target in the Makefile) plus CLI; or source-drop of hmp3/src
integration.min_toolchain: gcc/g++ with LTO for the Makefile (the L4cache fork built it with GCC 14.1.0 and Clang 18.1.6); MinGW cross builds for win32 (Pentium III, SSE) and win64; Visual Studio 2015 project files
integration.platforms: Linux x86-64 and ARM tested per README; Windows via MinGW or VS2015; requires IEEE-754 float (-DIEEE_FLOAT)
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. CMp3Enc holds per-encoder state, but emdct.c keeps MDCT tables in file-static arrays written at init and xhead.c keeps the Xing TOC in a file-static table, so concurrent encodes in one process are unsafe without care

gotchas: -B sets bitrate per channel: -B64 on stereo input is 128 kbps
Mixed C and C++ (bitallo*.cpp, mp3enc.cpp, srcc*.cpp) compiled through gcc and linked with -lstdc++, so it is not a pure-C library despite the catalog's language field

Builds with -march or -ffast-math produce slightly different MP3 files from the same input (L4cache 5.2.4 notes); in that fork, clang with znver4 plus fast-math ran about 1.5x slower (1.9x with PGO) than plain clang
-U2 switches the transform to the 'Pentium III' x-variants (xsbt_L3, xantialias), which on Linux are compiled C, not the original assembly
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick hmp3 over Shine when you want a floating-point encoder with a psychoacoustic model and VBR on desktop or server CPUs (Shine is fixed-point CBR, aimed at FPU-less hardware); pick SuperLAME instead when you need LAME's output and quality and want speed from multiple threads rather than a different encoder.
verified_claims_summary: Nothing measures hmp3 against LAME: the repository has no benchmark, and the 'about three times as fast as LAME' figure is Hydrogenaudio folklore about old Helix builds (search snippets only). The only numbers are the L4cache/hmp3 fork's 5.2.4 release notes, which time hmp3 builds against each other on an 85-minute (5103 s) 48 kHz stereo WAV on a Ryzen 7900X with GCC 14.1.0 and Clang 18.1.6, encoder settings not stated: 7.43 s (686.81x realtime) for plain gcc, 7.58 s for plain clang, 5.92 s (861.99x) for gcc with PGO, znver4 and fast-math.
status_note: Stale since 2024-05-31 (version 5.2.4, 38 stars, one maintainer, two open issues); usable and small, but the encoder sources are RPSL-1.0/RCSL with reciprocal source-release duties, so treat reuse as conditional even though the verifier rated it copyable.
sources_read: WebSearch: hmp3 Helix MP3 encoder speed versus LAME benchmark realtime (snippets: Hydrogenaudio wiki and forum, RareWares)
measurement_notes: No catalogued number to audit, so no correctness flaw behind numbers; D stands. Two more WebSearch passes found no hmp3-vs-LAME measurement beyond the Hydrogenaudio folklore. In the L4cache 5.2.4 table, the same source built with clang, znver4 and fast-math took 11.6 s (14.3 s with PGO) against 7.58 s for plain clang, an unexplained regression, and the notes say march and fast-math builds change the encoded output. Open issue #9 (2026-10-04, IgorCv2, AI-written patch) proposes LAME-style exhaustive Huffman partitioning: about 2% smaller MPEG-1 VBR files with bit-exact decoded PCM, at roughly 2x slower encoding, which would erode the speed edge if merged. Open issue #8 (2025-01-11): CBR init fails below about 48 kbps per channel. Language field: the encoder is mixed C and C++ with a C++ class API. No new leads.
